title: World Bank lifts Sri Lanka outlook, says recovery uneven | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 7 October 2026 05:46
-     - 32

World Bank Acting Country Manager for Sri Lanka Stephan Massing

World Bank Senior Economist Jakob Engel

The World Bank yesterday upgraded its outlook for Sri Lanka, raising its 2026 growth forecast to 4.4% from 3.6% in April, but warned that the recovery remains uneven, with poverty above pre-crisis levels and real wages still about 12% below 2019.

The latest in the Bank’s twice-yearly Sri Lanka Development Update, titled ‘From Recovery to Transformation’, projects growth easing to 4.2% in 2027 and 4% in 2028 as the post-crisis rebound fades and growth converges to its long-run trend amid weak productivity. The upgrade reflects the economy’s resilience to the Middle East conflict, though the forecast still marks a slowdown from 5% growth in both 2024 and 2025.

“Our baseline outlook represents an upgrade from the last edition,” World Bank Senior Economist Jakob Engel said, presenting the report at a media briefing in Colombo.

- Pix by Ruwan Walpola

World Bank...

The economy grew 4.7% year-on-year in the first half of 2026, its 12th consecutive quarter of expansion, returning GDP to its 2018 level. In July, the World Bank Group reclassified Sri Lanka as an upper middle-income country.

“Four years ago, Sri Lanka was confronting a deep and unprecedented economic crisis. Today, the news is that the economy has recovered to pre-crisis levels,” World Bank Acting Country Manager for Sri Lanka Stephan Massing said. “It has been growing for 12 consecutive quarters, and it has consistently been exceeding expectations, including our own projections.”

However, he cautioned that the gains have yet to reach many households. “What we have seen is recovery at the macroeconomic level that has not yet fully translated into recovery for ordinary families, for people across the country,” Massing said. “The challenge for Sri Lanka is no longer just economic recovery; it is economic transformation.”

How far growth can rise above the baseline depends on reform. Asked by the Daily FT whether the outlook reflected the economy’s current structural state or assumed reforms, Engel said the baseline assumed neither a major reform push nor any retreat from announced fiscal and trade policy plans.

“Our baseline outlook essentially assumes that current conditions continue into the future, so that we have about 4% growth,” he said. “If you have a big push on structural reforms, you could be looking at much higher growth rates of 5% or 6%.”

A significant weakening of fiscal discipline and more distortions in the economy would lower the outlook, he added. The Government’s medium-term growth target is 7%.

The baseline itself rests heavily on consumption. Private consumption is forecast to grow 4.7% in both 2026 and 2027 and 4.8% in 2028, while growth in fixed investment slows from 13.3% in 2025 to 6% this year and 3.8% by 2028. Imports are projected to outpace exports in each year of the forecast, with import growth rising to 6.3% by 2028 against export growth of 4.3%. Investment surged 25.5% in the first half, fuelled by private credit growth of 27.4% in June, much of it in personal loans, pawning and consumer durables.

That credit boom has also fed price pressures, which the Bank expects to ease only gradually. Inflation is forecast to average 5.7% this year, 5.3% in 2027 and return to the Central Bank’s 5% target in 2028, as the effects of higher energy prices and a weaker rupee work through the economy. Headline inflation reached 8% in August, breaching the 7% upper bound of the target band for a second month, prompting the Central Bank to raise its policy rate by 100 basis points to 8.75% in May, its first increase since 2023.

Energy costs are also weighing on the external accounts. The Bank projects a current account deficit of 0.5% of GDP this year, after a surplus of 1.6% in 2025, with deficits of 0.3% in 2027 and 0.4% in 2028, as imported energy inflates the import bill and key exports underperform. The current account swung to a deficit of $ 387 million in January to July, from a surplus of $ 1.7 billion a year earlier. Remittances are expected to remain the main counterweight. Gross reserves are projected to rise from 3.2 months of imports this year to 4.1 months by 2028, while net foreign direct investment is forecast to stay below 1% of GDP without major reforms to the investment climate.

The fiscal outlook is stronger. The primary surplus, which excludes interest payments, is projected at 3.9% of GDP this year, easing to 3.6% in 2027 and 3.5% in 2028, well above the 2.6% targeted in the Government’s Fiscal Strategy Statement. The overall deficit is forecast to narrow from 2.6% of GDP to 2.1% over the period, while revenue and grants hold at around 16.4% to 16.6% of GDP.

On that basis, central Government debt is projected to fall from 87% of GDP this year to 81.9% in 2027 and 77.2% in 2028, and public and publicly guaranteed debt to 86.2% by 2028. Interest payments, which absorbed 46% of revenue in 2025, are expected to fall to about 34% by 2028.

Part of the fiscal outperformance, however, reflects money not spent. Only 16.7% of the 2026 capital budget and 8% of the Rs. 500 billion allocated for Cyclone Ditwah reconstruction had been disbursed by mid-year, which the Bank attributed to weaknesses in project selection, procurement and implementation rather than financing constraints. Public spending is expected to remain muted under the 13%-of-GDP primary expenditure ceiling set by the Public Financial Management Act.

These macroeconomic gains are expected to reach households only slowly. Poverty at the $ 4.20-a-day line is projected to fall from 16.9% in 2025 to 15.8% this year, 14.8% in 2027 and 14% in 2028, still above the 11.5% of 2019. At the $ 8.30-a-day line, more relevant for an upper middle-income country, the rate is forecast to decline from 59.1% this year to 55.7% in 2028. Higher prices will slow poverty reduction this year, the Bank said, with labour force participation and real wages still below pre-crisis levels.

The Bank said risks to the outlook are tilted to the downside. These include prolonged energy market volatility, weaker global growth, reform setbacks and a strong El Niño, which forecasters give a greater than 90% probability and which could hit harvests, infrastructure and food prices into 2028. On the upside, faster structural reforms, a de-escalation in the Middle East, milder weather and a quicker recovery in tourism could lift growth and accelerate poverty reduction.

To move beyond the baseline, the Bank called for a new growth model in which private investment, exports and productivity, rather than public spending, drive growth. This would require stronger infrastructure and fiscal and external buffers, a predictable business environment, an end to anti-export bias, and private finance in sectors such as agribusiness, tourism, logistics and digital.

Agribusiness, the report’s special focus, illustrates both the potential and the obstacles. While primary agriculture accounts for 8.4% of GDP, the broader agrifood system, including processing, logistics, trade and food services, accounts for an estimated 17.3% of GDP and 42% of employment. Agriculture and food products made up 31.4% of goods exports in 2025, worth $ 4 billion, led by tea at $ 1.5 billion and coconut-related products at over $ 1 billion. Food processing generates about five times the value added per worker of primary agriculture.

Yet policy has penalised exporters. Between 2013 and 2022, tea growers were effectively taxed by about 33% and coconut growers by 42%, while potato and onion growers enjoyed protection of over 50%. Tea output is about 25% below its 2013 peak, with replanting at just 17% of the recommended rate in 2022.

The Bank recommended reforming export cess levies on tea and coconut, making tariff changes predictable, redirecting subsidies towards research and climate-smart agriculture, operationalising the National Single Window and cold-chain infrastructure, and extending plantation leases beyond 2045. It estimated that fully eliminating para-tariffs, which the Government plans to phase out by 2029, could raise exports by up to 11% and real GDP by about 4.7% in the long run.

“Sri Lanka’s story for the last four years has been one of recovery. The story for the next four years should be one of opportunity,” Massing said.

The report accompanies the World Bank’s South Asia Economic Update, ‘Adopting AI for Growth’, which projects regional growth rising to 6.9% this year.

title: Only 16.7% of capital Budget, 8% of Ditwah funds spent by  mid-year: World Bank | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 7 October 2026 05:45
-     - 15

The Government had spent only 16.7% of its 2026 capital Budget and about 8% of the Rs. 500 billion allocated for Cyclone Ditwah reconstruction by mid-year, the World Bank said yesterday. It attributed the shortfall to weak public investment management rather than a lack of funds.

In its Sri Lanka Development Update, the Bank said the under-execution reflects weaknesses in project selection, procurement and implementation capacity, rather than financing constraints. A similar pattern was evident in other crisis spending, with less than half of the Rs. 100 billion Middle East war relief package disbursed by mid-year.

The shortfall has flattered the fiscal accounts. Revenue rose 27.2% year-on-year in the first half, while spending grew only 7.9%. The primary surplus, which excludes interest payments, reached Rs. 1.2 trillion, about Rs. 360 billion higher than a year earlier. The overall budget recorded a surplus of Rs. 9.5 billion, against a deficit of Rs. 406 billion in the first half of 2025.

The Bank said improving the quality of spending matters more than raising its level, because the Government cannot simply spend more. The fiscal space created by lower interest costs and stronger revenue cannot be channelled into higher primary spending without breaching the 13%-of-GDP primary expenditure ceiling under the Public Financial Management Act.

With the spending envelope essentially fixed, the Bank said better project selection, procurement and execution are the main means of increasing the growth impact of public spending. It called for a more systematic approach to project screening, risk filtering, prioritisation and appraisal to reduce cost and time overruns.

The Bank expects public spending to remain muted, with primary surpluses of at least 3.5% of GDP over the medium term. That is well above the 2.6% targeted from 2027 in the Government’s Fiscal Strategy Statement. Interest payments, which absorbed 46% of revenue in 2025, are projected to fall to about 34% by 2028, down from a crisis peak of almost 80%.

The Bank noted that with a solid primary surplus and spending already constrained, the Government may consider using part of its fiscal space to unwind some of the regressivity in Sri Lanka’s tax mix.

title: Poverty declining, but still above pre-crisis levels: World Bank | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 7 October 2026 05:45
-     - 10

Poverty in Sri Lanka is recovering but remains above pre-crisis levels, the World Bank said yesterday. It projected a gradual decline to 14% by 2028, which would still leave the rate above 2019, and warned that the recovery is uneven across the country.

In its October Sri Lanka Development Update, the Bank estimated poverty at 16.9% in 2025, measured at the $ 4.20-a-day line for lower middle-income countries. That is down from a crisis peak of 20.7% in 2023 but above the 11.5% of 2019. The rate is projected to fall to 15.8% this year and 14.8% in 2027.

“Our main finding is that Sri Lanka’s economic recovery continues. It is real, and many households are still waiting to feel it,” World Bank Senior Economist Jakob Engel said at a media briefing in Colombo.

The 2023 peak reflects a new methodology that sharply lowers the Bank’s earlier estimates, which had put it at 27.6%. The 2024 estimate falls to 18.4% from 25%, the 2025 now cast to 16.9% from 22.1%, and the 2028 projection to 14% from 18.9%. At the national poverty line, the 2023 peak is revised to 24% from 31.4%.

In an explanatory note, the Bank stressed that the revision does not mean poverty has fallen by about 7 percentage points. “Poverty on the ground has not changed, it is now measured more accurately,” it said. The 2019 baseline is unchanged, and poverty still roughly doubled during the crisis, pushing an estimated two million people below the poverty line.

The revision stems from a seven-year gap in official data, since the last Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES) was conducted in 2019. The Bank’s earlier estimates filled that gap by simulating household welfare from national accounts data, assuming price increases passed almost fully to households. The new estimates instead draw on the annual Labour Force Survey (LFS), which records actual employment, labour incomes and household composition.

The Bank said the results were calibrated against the 2016 and 2019 HIES and corroborated by independent surveys from the International Food Policy Research Institute, the World Food Programme, LirneAsia and its own 2024 phone survey. The International Food Policy Research Institute’s survey, for instance, put poverty at about 15.4% at the $ 4.20 line for 2025.

The Bank cautioned, however, that the revised figures are not official statistics and should be read as a trend rather than precise point estimates. The HIES, produced by the Department of Census and Statistics, remains the official benchmark. The estimates will be updated when 2025 LFS data become available in November, and again when the 2025 HIES is released in 2027.

Whatever the measure, the underlying indicators point to deep and lasting damage. Real labour incomes fell by more than 40% between 2019 and 2023 and, despite a partial recovery, real wages remain about 12% below 2019 levels. Labour force participation fell from 52.3% in 2019 to 47.4% in 2024 before recovering to 49.4% in 2025, while female participation, at 32.4%, remains among the lowest in the region. Stunting among children under five rose from 7.4% in 2021 to 10.1% in 2025.

The recovery is also highly uneven. Poverty outside the Western Province is two to three times higher than within it, and reached 36% in the estate sector in 2024. The poverty gap, the average shortfall between what poor households have and what they need to meet basic needs, doubled nationally between 2019 and 2024 and is four times larger in the Northern Province than in the Western Province. The Bank warned that in more deprived regions, crisis losses risk becoming difficult to reverse or even permanent.

Households also remain exposed to new shocks, with two-fifths of Sri Lankans either poor or living within 50% of the poverty line. Higher energy costs linked to the Middle East conflict stalled the recovery in real incomes in the first half of 2026. Transport costs, a largely unavoidable expense for informal and low-skilled workers, have risen about 21%, while public sector wages have fallen again in real terms.

“Real wages are still lower than they were before the crisis, and many families have been impacted by recent shocks, such as Cyclone Ditwah, and they remain vulnerable to future shocks,” World Bank Acting Country Manager for Sri Lanka Stephan Massing said.

The Bank also cautioned against reading Sri Lanka’s reclassification as an upper middle-income country in July as evidence of a broad recovery, since the classification is based on national average income per capita, which does not reflect how income is distributed. “These are two different measures and should not be read together as a single story of recovery,” it said.

At the $ 8.30-a-day line for upper middle-income countries, poverty stood at 61.1% in 2025 and is projected to fall only to 55.7% by 2028. The Bank described the line as an aspirational benchmark for now. Extreme poverty, at the $ 3-a-day line, is projected to decline from 6% to 4.9% over the same period.

The findings put the focus on social protection. The Bank said the Aswesuma program, expanded during the crisis to cover at least the poorest 20% of the population, has improved targeting and coverage, especially in the estate sector. However, targeting still needs improvement and the system remains slow to scale up support when new shocks hit, which the Bank called a key policy priority.

The Bank expects growth to support a recovery in real wages and labour force participation over the medium term, though progress this year will be slowed by Cyclone Ditwah, higher inflation and households’ depleted savings.

title: CPC sees fuel prices holding through Oct., steps up precautionary imports | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 7 October 2026 05:43
-     - 10

The Ceylon Petroleum Corporation (CPC) yesterday said current fuel prices can be maintained until the end of October and assured that the country has adequate stocks, while moving to secure additional shipments as a precautionary measure.

Addressing the media, CPC Chairman D.J. Rajakaruna said the Corporation was also confident of maintaining the current fuel price and supply situation over the next three months, provided there were no major unforeseen disruptions.

“There is no issue with fuel stocks,” he said, while urging motorists not to panic over reports of shortages or form unnecessary queues at filling stations.

He said CPC reviews its fuel stocks every Tuesday and that the latest assessment had found no concerns over available reserves. Nevertheless, arrangements had been made to expedite two additional fuel shipments, while imports exceeding the country’s requirements for October were also being secured as a precaution.

Rajakaruna said any temporary shortages being experienced in certain areas were linked mainly to other fuel companies reducing supplies to their filling stations, rather than an overall shortage in the country.

Around 62 areas, where such shortages could potentially occur had been identified about three weeks ago, he said, following which arrangements were made with the relevant companies to increase supplies to those locations.

“If fuel shortages or long queues are reported at stations operated by other companies, the public can use the nearest CPC filling station,” he said.

The CPC Chairman stressed that there was no reason to expect a major countrywide fuel shortage and appealed to motorists to avoid precautionary buying, which could itself create unnecessary queues and localised supply pressure.

title: PM rings Bell at CSE to champion financial literacy, investor education | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 7 October 2026 05:41
-     - 13

As part of World Investor Week (WIW) 2026, the Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka (SEC) and the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) joined stock exchanges around the world in ringing the market opening bell for financial literacy on 5 October 2026, under the patronage of Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya.

World Investor Week is an annual global campaign led by the International Organisation of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) to raise awareness of the importance of investor education and investor protection. The “Ring the Bell for Financial Literacy” initiative, pioneered by the World Federation of Exchanges (WFE), brings together stock exchanges and other stakeholders worldwide to promote greater financial literacy and encourage individuals to make informed financial decisions.

The ceremony also marked the 40th anniversary of the CSE and the joint launch by the SEC and the CSE of the Stock Market Game, an online stock market simulation based on the ATrad trading system.

The Stock Market Game enables participants to gain practical experience of how the stock market works, make investment decisions and construct portfolios of listed shares without using real money. The platform is accessible through the websites of the SEC and CSE and is expected to serve as an important practical tool for promoting financial education. It is envisaged that the Stock Market Game will also be used to conduct simulation competitions among universities and the 100 Capital Market Clubs established in schools across the country.

The ceremony also featured the commemorative issuance of a stamp and First Day Cover to mark the 40th anniversary of the CSE. Issued in collaboration with the Department of Posts and the Philatelic Bureau of Sri Lanka, the commemorative stamp and First Day Cover were presented to Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya, by the SEC Chairman Senior Prof. D.B.P.H. Dissabandara and CSE Director and Central Depository Systems (CDS) Chairman Ray Abeywardena.

Delivering the keynote address, Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya commended the efforts of the SEC and CSE in promoting financial literacy and highlighted the importance of strengthening the capital market and creating new investment opportunities for the younger generation.

“As the CSE commemorates its 40th anniversary, the Government commends its continued efforts to promote and strengthen financial literacy across the country. We are committed to moving beyond traditional savings schemes, strengthening the capital market and developing new investment opportunities for the younger generation.

“I urge our youth to think differently—to seize opportunities rather than simply wait for them, to actively seek out new possibilities and, more importantly, to create opportunities of their own.

“Do not focus only on achieving high marks in examinations. Develop sound financial knowledge and skills that will serve you throughout your life. I also encourage you to challenge yourselves to become responsible and empowered citizens who can contribute to building stronger communities and a stronger economy.”

Welcoming the gathering, CSE CEO Rajeeva Bandaranaike highlighted the importance of obtaining reliable information when making investment decisions.

“We operate in a digital world where a vast amount of information and data is disseminated through social media. While some of this information is factual, some may be inaccurate or misleading. When investing in the stock market, it is essential to make informed and prudent investment decisions. Therefore, investors should obtain information and data from reliable and responsible sources and persons before making investment decisions.”

SEC Chairman Senior Prof. Dissabandara emphasised that the SEC’s role extends beyond regulation to facilitating the further development of the capital market.

“The SEC needs to determine how best to introduce the stock market to Generation Alpha, Generation Beta and generations beyond. When it comes to investors, we need to build confidence in the market, because people will invest only when they have confidence in the market.

“The Stock Market Game we are introducing today is not only an initiative to promote financial literacy, but can also contribute to greater financial inclusion. Although financial literacy levels are around 58%, the number of people who have invested in the capital market remains significantly lower.

“While we have come a long way, there is still much more to be done. There are around 200,000 registered companies in the country, yet only 291 are listed on the stock market. This highlights the significant potential for further development and expansion of our capital market.”

To coincide with World Investor Week, the SEC and CSE have lined up a series of initiatives aimed at enhancing financial literacy, promoting greater awareness of the capital market and encouraging wider retail investor participation. 

These include setting up an investor education stall at the World Trade Centre Colombo to provide tenants with information on investing in the capital market; participating in the Financial Literacy Expo organised by the Central Bank of Sri Lanka; and televising “Madura’s Bamboo Flute Dream,” an animated educational series for children, on Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation. In addition, a nationwide campaign will be conducted across 14 locations countrywide, with the aim of expanding retail investor participation and facilitating the opening of 10,000 new CDS accounts.

The event was attended by a wide range of capital market stakeholders, including Commission  members of the SEC, Board Members of the CSE, senior officials of both the SEC and CSE, officials from the Ministry of Education, CEOs of stockbroker firms and unit trust management companies, Vice Chancellors of national universities, principals and students representing Stock Market Clubs, and other distinguished guests from across the financial and academic sectors

title: Cabinet approves Visa Waiver Agreement between Sri Lanka and Thailand | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 7 October 2026 05:40
-     - 12

The Cabinet of Ministers has approved the signing of a Visa Waiver Agreement for Ordinary Passport Holders between the Governments of Sri Lanka and Thailand.

Announcing the decision at the weekly post-Cabinet meeting media briefing yesterday, Cabinet Spokesman and Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa said the agreement is aimed at further strengthening the friendly relations between the two countries and making travel easier for their citizens.

“Under its terms, citizens of both countries holding valid ordinary passports will be able to enter, exit and transit the other country without a prior visa. Each stay may last up to 30 days, with a cumulative stay of no more than 90 days within any period of 180 days,” he explained.

Dr. Jayatissa said the waiver applies to general tourism only. “It does not cover employment, education, media work or any other activity that requires prior approval,” he added.

The proposal to this effect was submitted by Public Security and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Ananda Wijepala.

title: Govt. eases capital outflow curbs, keeps Bond plans under wraps | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 7 October 2026 05:37
-     - 21

Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Deputy Minister Chathuranga Abeysinghe

The Government yesterday defended its gradual opening of the capital account and refused to disclose its plans for Sri Lanka’s international Bonds, arguing that any such signal would be market-sensitive.

Responding in Parliament during the debate on new regulations governing foreign exchange outflows, Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Deputy Minister Chathuranga Abeysinghe said the measures would boost investor confidence by easing restrictions on capital leaving the country.

Under the changes, local companies can invest abroad up to $ 750,000 without prior approval from the Central Bank. Abeysinghe said the allowance for Sri Lankans who emigrate had also been revised, while larger transfers would remain subject to approval.

“We have gradually opened up over the last two years. We have opened the entire import market and now we are opening the capital market,” he said, adding that returning to pre-crisis levels of openness would take time.

He contrasted the approach with that of former President Ranil Wickremesinghe, arguing that the previous administration built reserves by contracting the economy through higher taxes and curbs on imports and the capital account. “If you do that, any country can save foreign exchange. We are not doing that,” he said.

Abeysinghe rejected Opposition calls for the Government to state whether it would buy back or issue Bonds, saying decisions on International Sovereign Bonds (ISBs) would be made by the Finance Ministry and the Public Debt Management Office (PDMO). “Asking the Government to say whether it is going to buy or issue Bonds is asking it to disclose market-sensitive information,” he said, adding that bondholders need not be informed of the Government’s plans in advance.

“We have a strong plan to manage our debt, and we are confident in the officials in the Ministry,” he said.

Turning to the fiscal position, Abeysinghe dismissed claims that revenue gains were driven mainly by vehicle imports. He said Government revenue had risen from 13.5% to 16.7% of GDP, with vehicle imports contributing about 1.2 percentage points, and that such revenue would continue this year.

He said Sri Lanka had accumulated more than $ 1.5 billion in reserves for the fourth consecutive year and was on track to close 2026 with about $ 8 billion. Citing the IMF’s seventh review, the last before the program concludes, he said the Fund had acknowledged the economy’s remarkable resilience in withstanding successive shocks, including the global downturn and US tariff changes.

Abeysinghe also accused the 2015–2019 administration of raising costly ISBs at around 7% interest in 2015 and 2016, and said its Foreign Exchange Act had created loopholes that enabled capital flight.

He added that Parliament was also approving an ADB loan to be disbursed to the SME sector.

title: Harsha urges MLB buy-back to save up to $ 400 m | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 7 October 2026 05:32
-     - 27

SJB MP Dr. Harsha de Silva

Samagi Jana Balawegaya (SJB) MP Dr. Harsha de Silva yesterday urged the Government to buy back part of Sri Lanka’s Macro-Linked Bonds (MLBs) before markets reprice them, claiming proactive action could save the country $ 300 million to $ 400 million over the next decade.

MLBs, issued under the 2024 sovereign debt restructuring, tie repayments to economic performance, so that bondholders recover more if GDP growth exceeds the IMF baseline. Dr. de Silva told Parliament that because growth has surpassed that forecast, total payments on the instruments would rise from $ 6.2 billion to $ 7.4 billion over the next 10 years if the Public Debt Management Office (PDMO) does nothing.

“If we wait, the market is going to reprice these Bonds, and we will no longer have an incentive to buy them back,” he said. “We have to play the market before the market plays us.”

The legal framework for such an operation already exists, he noted, pointing to the 2018 Liability Management Act he proposed as a Non-Cabinet Minister. The potential saving, he added, was about twice the $ 200 million Asian Development Bank (ADB) loan before the House.

Dr. de Silva conceded the MLB terms were unfavourable, but argued the deal had taken Sri Lanka out of default and into a stable position, and that the task now was to manage the liability efficiently. He faulted the PDMO for being slow to decide how the country would return to international capital markets.

That urgency, he argued, was underscored by a debt reduction story the Government was overstating. Public debt to GDP stood at 98% at end-2025 and was expected to fall to about 93%, a positive he said must be acknowledged. However, most of the reduction occurred between 2022 and 2024, when the ratio fell from 121%, on the back of revenue, spending and restructuring decisions taken before the present Government assumed office.

Nor, he said, was the higher-than-expected primary surplus entirely a product of discipline. Only 76% of capital expenditure was executed in 2025, and just 26% from January to August this year. “Underspending is not the same thing as fiscal reform, and it costs us growth,” he said, adding that the President’s pledge to spend over 4% of GDP on capital investment must actually be implemented.

Revenue gains were similarly flattered by one-off factors. Dr. de Silva said Rs. 900 billion, or 63%, of the Rs. 1.4 trillion revenue increase in 2025 came from pent-up demand for vehicle imports, which was not sustainable beyond this year. Citing Fitch, he said interest payments were expected to absorb about 41% of Government revenue this year, while external repayments would rise after 2028 to about $ 4 billion a year by 2030, leaving the country vulnerable to external shocks.

Against those heavy repayments, he said, new financing remained thin. Excluding the IMF, multilateral lenders disbursed only about $ 177 million in the first half of 2026: the World Bank $ 94 million, ADB $ 52 million, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank $ 23 million and others $ 8 million. Bilateral lenders disbursed just $ 24 million, led by Japan at about $ 14 million and India at $ 8 million, while the IMF disbursed about $ 619 million over the same period.

“Six months of near-zero bilateral inflows is not a financing strategy,” he said.

Even where funds were secured, Dr. de Silva questioned the Government’s capacity to use them. He asked how the $ 45 million budgeted this year under the $ 200 million ADB facility would be spent with 10 months already lapsed. He also termed the Finance Ministry’s $ 57.4 million ADB agreement to promote rooftop solar through virtual net metering an ‘oxymoron’, given the Government’s stated position of ending net metering. “One part of the Government can’t say we are stopping rooftop solar while another part obtains ADB funding to promote it,” he said.

Such inconsistencies, he warned, would also weigh on market access, which the recent upgrade to ‘B-‘ did not guarantee. He noted that only Fitch had upgraded Sri Lanka and that a rating of at least ‘BB’ was needed, adding that the upgrade reflected past reforms while further improvement would depend on the Government’s forward policies.

He observed that the Government had acknowledged IMF funding was conditional on the Budget conforming to the program, meaning the Government would remain aligned with the IMF throughout 2027.

Turning finally to reserves, Dr. de Silva said they had recovered but remained well below the IMF’s Assessing Reserve Adequacy (ARA) metric, with net usable reserves lower than publicly stated as they included swaps that could not be drawn on. Central Bank dollar purchases fell from almost $ 600 million in August to $ 65 million in September, he said, stressing that sustained purchases and policy consistency were essential to improving ratings and regaining market access.

title: EDB directs Trinco SMEs towards export markets | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 7 October 2026 05:20
-     - 13

The Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB), operating under the Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Ministry, conducted a ‘SME Awareness Creation Forum’ at the Trincomalee District Secretariat on 1 October 2026. 

The forum aimed to support and develop regional small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and entrepreneurs with export potential in the Trincomalee District of Eastern Province. The program comprised three main components; an awareness creation seminar, a mini exhibition and a business clinic.

At the seminar, entrepreneurs learned about EDB services, export market requirements and opportunities, and heard success stories from the fruits and vegetables, processed foods, handicraft and lifestyle products, and fisheries products sectors.

The mini exhibition showcased exportable products from these sectors, with stakeholder institutions and export companies taking part. At the business clinic, EDB officials, public and private stakeholders provided support to help entrepreneurs address their individual challenges and develop products that meet international market standards.

The Trincomalee District of Eastern Province was selected in line with strategic export development priorities, with a focus on integrating fisheries and marine products, agricultural products and tourism-related enterprises into export value chains.

The forum was held as part of the EDB’s regional outreach program under the National Export Development Plan (NEDP), which aims to bring export promotion closer to regional entrepreneurs and connect them with global value chains. Nine such forums have been held across the country since 2017, most recently in Batticaloa in February 2025. The forum is expected to identify export-ready companies in the region and develop them as future exporters.

It also aimed to attract local investment for export industries, raise awareness of the New Exporter Development Program among Government officials, trade chambers and other stakeholders, and encourage innovative, value-added products for export markets.

Through such programs, the EDB will continue to take export promotion to the regions and promote regional economic development.

The program was attended by Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Minister Sunil Handunnetti, Foreign Affairs and Foreign Employment Deputy Minister Arun Hemachandra, Trincomalee District Member of Parliament Roshan Akmeemana, Trincomalee District Secretary Hemantha Kumara, EDB Chairman/Chief Executive Officer Mangala Wijesinghe, Provincial Director of the Eastern Province Department of Rural Industries Riswani Rifas, Divisional Secretaries, and EDB Director of Regional Development D. M. P. Dissanayake, along with officials of the EDB and other State institutions, exporters and a large number of entrepreneurs.

Addressing the gathering, Minister Handunnetti said that any task appears impossible until it is accomplished, and that if one gives up believing it cannot be done, it can never be achieved.

The Minister also said that Trincomalee has a unique natural harbour unlike any other in the world, a large extent of land still unused for industry, and vast mineral resources in areas such as Kokkilai, Pudavakattu and Pulmoddai and in the ocean. He pointed out that once the expressway from Colombo to Dambulla is completed, the districts of the Eastern Province will become key areas with the infrastructure required for industry, employment and land. He also stressed that such big dreams can be realised by starting as small businesses and working together.

title: NCEL and COOPFED sign MoU for supply of essential food commodities | Daily FT

The National Co-operative Exports Limited (NCEL), India, and the Sri Lanka Consumer Co-operative Societies Federation Limited (COOPFED) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in Colombo today to strengthen cooperation in the supply of essential commodities, food security and cooperative development.

The MoU was signed by NCEL Managing Director Unupom Kausik and COOPFED Chairman Dr. Shantha Jayarathne in the presence of Trade, Commerce, Food Security and Cooperative Development Minister Wasantha Samarasinghe and Indian High Commissioner Santosh Jha.

The MoU provides a framework for leveraging the cooperative networks and expertise of the two organisations. Under this partnership, essential food items will be supplied from India to Sri Lanka through the cooperative networks of NCEL and help minimise shortages and improve availability at affordable prices.

In addition to the supply of agricultural and food commodities, the MoU envisages cooperation in the exchange of market information and best practices, capacity building, technical cooperation, warehousing and logistics, supply-chain management and digital platforms. It will also strengthen institutional linkages between the cooperative sectors of the two countries.NCEL is established under the aegis of the India’s Ministry of Cooperation, to promote exports from the cooperative sector. Its partnership with COOPFED, the apex federation of consumer cooperative societies in Sri Lanka, will strengthen linkages between Indian suppliers and Sri Lankan consumers. The signing of the MoU marks a further step in strengthening India–Sri Lanka economic ties with a focus on food security, resilient supply chains and benefits for producers and consumers.

title: Sri Lanka’s homegrown delivery platform ‘Ting’ unveils multi-vendor ordering and built-in bill splitting | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 7 October 2026 05:18
-     - 22

Sri Lanka’s delivery landscape is about to take a different direction. Ting, a homegrown innovation-first platform, built for Sri Lankan ordering habits, will officially launch on 30 October 2026 in the Colombo district, introducing a new approach to food delivery designed around how people actually order together rather than how traditional delivery apps have operated.

‘Ting’ is part of Edine Services Ltd., a fully Sri Lankan-owned platform services company. Launching under the brand promise ‘Ting – the one ting for everything,’ the platform combines multiple firsts from day one, including multi-vendor ordering, built-in bill splitting, and a managed rider fleet, trained for consistent service quality, creating a more seamless experience for customers, merchants and riders.

Unlike conventional delivery platforms that require separate orders from different restaurants, Ting’s multi-vendor capability allows customers to place a single order from multiple merchants and a multitude of categories within one basket, proceed to checkout and ability to track the experience through a single view. Whether it is a main meal from one restaurant, dessert from another and groceries for home, the platform removes the need to switch between multiple apps, payments and deliveries.

Group ordering has also been designed as a core feature rather than an add-on. Customers can choose to have one person host the payment, split the bill equally among friends, or allow each person to pay only for what they ordered, while keeping the entire order together and delivered to one location.

Beyond the app experience, Ting is also introducing its own managed rider fleet from launch. Riders are trained in service and customer experience, equipped with branded gear, and supported through Ting’s dedicated Rider Hub. Service quality will be maintained through structured training and ongoing performance support, creating greater consistency for both merchants and customers. 

As the platform expands, Ting also plans to introduce opportunities for riders to join the platform on a freelance basis, providing greater flexibility for those looking to earn through delivery work.

Edine Services Ltd. Assistant General Manager - Business Operations and Marketing Nayanapriya Dias said, “We set out to build a platform around the way Sri Lankans actually order today, together, across different preferences and with growing expectations for greater convenience. Ting brings these needs into one connected experience, providing merchants a more consistent and financially supportive commercial structure and riders a structured operating environment. Our ambition is to build a distinctly Sri Lankan platform which can continue to evolve with the market.”

The initial rollout will begin across the Colombo district, with additional platform developments and service enhancements, and geographic expansion set to follow as Ting expands its roadmap after the launch.

With its official launch, Ting represents a new chapter in Sri Lanka’s homegrown digital delivery, introducing features designed to simplify everyday ordering while creating long-term value across the delivery ecosystem.

For more information, visit https://ting.lk/. The Ting app is available for download on the Apple App Store and Google Play.

title: Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Sri Lanka kicks off today | Daily FT

Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Sri Lanka opens today at Cinnamon Life, bringing fashion, design and luxury experiences into the heart of Colombo. 

Presented by AOD and powered by DIMO, the week brings together emerging talent, established designers, business leaders and the Mercedes-Benz community, united by a shared ambition for the city’s future. 

As DIMO and AOD look towards a decade of partnership in 2027, this year’s edition opens a conversation about what comes next. The opportunity is to build on Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Sri Lanka’s platform, connecting Sri Lankan creativity with international audiences and giving Colombo a distinctive place in the region’s fashion and lifestyle calendar. 

DIMO’s role is central to that ambition, bringing Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week to Sri Lanka and the brand into a cultural setting where design, personal style and relationships matter. It also gives the Mercedes-Benz community new occasions to meet, exchange ideas and experience the city together. For DIMO, building this community is part of delivering the Mercedes-Benz lifestyle in Sri Lanka. Through fashion, conversation and carefully curated experiences, the brand becomes part of people’s lives, interests and aspirations. 

The launch of “She’s Mercedes” in Sri Lanka during Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Sri Lanka adds a new dimension to that relationship, creating a space for women to connect and contribute to its future. 

DIMO Executive Director Rajeev Pandithage said:  “Mercedes-Benz, with over 140 years of innovation, represents a way of life that cannot simply be purchased from a showroom. At DIMO, we bring that world to life through the experiences we create, the community we build and the expert care we provide throughout the ownership journey. From personalised service to trusted technical expertise, every interaction reflects a commitment to the standards Mercedes-Benz owners expect. Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Sri Lanka is part of that commitment, connecting people through a shared appreciation of design, culture and exceptional lifestyle experiences. That relationship begins with an interest in the brand and grows well beyond ownership.” 

From AOD’s perspective, the partnership connects creative talent with an audience that can help it grow. Designers need visibility, but they also need customers, commissions, commercial relationships and people willing to invest in their ideas. Bringing creativity into the same room as business leaders and an affluent, internationally connected community creates the conditions for those relationships to begin. AOD’s role is to conceive and build that platform, drawing on its work in design education and the creative industries. 

As it marks 25 years in 2026, Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Sri Lanka gives that work a public stage, placing new talent alongside established creative businesses and showing how education can lead into enterprise. 

AOD Founder and Chairperson Linda Speldewinde said: “Innovation needs places where creative ideas meet people who can help realise them. Our partnership with DIMO brings designers into a community that values design and can become their customers, collaborators and investors. For us, the substance of Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Sri Lanka lies in those connections and what they make possible: stronger creative businesses, new opportunities for talent and a more ambitious future for Colombo.”

Fashion and the city economy 

The economic opportunity extends across Colombo. A compelling programme gives people a reason to spend time in the city, stay in its hotels, dine in its restaurants, shop and take part in its evening life. Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Sri Lanka can connect these experiences, encouraging visitors and residents to explore more of what Colombo has to offer. Behind every runway is another network of economic activity: designers, garment makers, models, stylists, photographers, production crews and event suppliers. A sustained fashion platform can generate work across that network while helping local labels reach buyers and develop their businesses. The longer-term ambition is to turn that activity into a stronger creative economy. A recognisable annual calendar can help businesses plan around the event, encourage partnerships across sectors and build international interest over time. For Colombo, the value lies in developing experiences that people want to return for, supported by creative businesses capable of growing with that demand. Luxury also has a role in this conversation. Fashion, hospitality and the Mercedes-Benz community bring together audiences who value design, service and distinctive experiences. Connecting them with Sri Lankan creative enterprise opens possibilities for patronage, collaboration and investment, while giving local talent access to new markets.

Bringing the business community into the conversation 

The Daily FT’s partnership forms part of the wider support of Wijeya Newspapers, whose other media titles also help bring Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Sri Lanka to audiences across the country. That collective support gives the event a broader public presence and helps tell the stories of the people and businesses behind it. 

The Daily FT has a particular role in connecting fashion and creativity with the business community. Its coverage provides a place to examine the commercial potential of design, the opportunities for investment and the contribution that a more active creative sector can make to Colombo’s growth. This opening-day partnership therefore looks beyond the programme itself. It brings a business perspective to the ambition shared by DIMO and AOD: to build a platform that supports creative enterprise, strengthens relationships across industries and helps make Colombo a more vibrant, internationally connected city. Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Sri Lanka begins today with the runway as its focal point. As DIMO and AOD approach their next decade together, the wider opportunity is to carry that energy into the city, creating relationships and business opportunities that continue long after the Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Sri Lanka ends.

title: Cabinet approves 1,050 official email accounts for 350 Courts under ‘e-Court’ digitisation drive | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 7 October 2026 05:25
-     - 5

The Cabinet of Ministers has approved providing official email facilities to Courts across the country, as part of the ‘e-Court’ digitalisation project. 

The e-Court project was approved at the Cabinet meeting held on 15 December 2025. As a first step, digital systems are being created for case file management in the Magistrate’s Courts, District Courts and High Courts. Official email is a basic requirement for this, and it must be available to officers at all levels of the judicial system.

“Under the approved proposal, 1,050 official email accounts will be provided to 350 Courts at the initial stage. The accounts will be set up under the Government Official Information Portal (gov.lk) with the official domain name courts.gov.lk,” Cabinet Spokesman and Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa said at the weekly post-Cabinet meeting media briefing yesterday.

He said the hosting for the accounts will be provided through the email system currently used by the Justice and National Integration Ministry.

The email system will also include voice-to-text and video conferencing facilities. The voice-to-text feature will convert oral statements into documents on the spot, and has been identified as a solution to the current shortage of stenographers in the courts.

The video conferencing facility supports the online hearing of cases. Under the Criminal Procedure Code (Amendment) Act No. 7 of 2025 and the Victims and Witnesses of Crime (Support and Protection) Act No. 4 of 2015, video conferencing facilities must be provided to all courts.

The proposal to this effect was submitted by Justice and National Integration Minister Harshana Nanayakkara.

By Tisaranee Gunasekara

“In this country, even an animal shouldn’t go hungry.” NPP presidential election ad about street dogs (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PvjmRn3rYug) 

A group of young people walk into a café. When the owner realises that one of them is blind, he presents her with a menu in braille. “What made you think of us?” she asks in wonder. “When I opened the shop, I thought of everyone,” the owner replies. “Are you a member of the Compass (NPP)?” she asks. “Yes, Miss,” he answers (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VxmIAWztYgc). 

Knowingly or not, this and other NPP presidential election ads harked back to philosopher John Rawls’ famous thought experiment on how to build a fair and just society for all. Contained in his 1971 book, A Theory of Justice, the experiment imagines a situation where people have a chance of building the society they will eventually live in, but must do so from behind a Veil of Ignorance preventing them from knowing their place in that society. The best solution is to build a universally just society based on two pillars: the liberty principle ensuring that everyone has the maximum freedom without intruding on another’s freedom; and the difference principle ensuring that everyone has an equal opportunity to succeed. 

That was in effect the NPP’s 2024 promise: a new Sri Lanka in which all her people could live in freedom and dignity.

Is this the direction in which the Compass is turned?

Sri Lanka’s recovery from the havoc of Gotabaya-economics began and reached the key milestone of positive growth during the Ranil Wickremesinghe presidency. But a disproportionate share of the burden of this recovery was borne by those who could least afford it. Correcting this imbalance, and rebuilding Sri Lanka as a more just and liveable place was the NPP’s pledge to the electorate. 

And yet, two years on, the fundamentals of socio-economic injustice remain unchanged, untouched, unconsidered. While high indirect taxes continue to hike living costs, the Government is mulling over a cut in direct taxes. Increasing PAYE threshold from the current Rs. 150,000 to Rs. 200,000 is reportedly under consideration. 

92% of formal private sector employees in Sri Lanka earn less than Rs. 100,000 a month. The proposed tax cut will thus benefit only a thin sliver of high-earning private sector employees. The reduced revenue will have to be recouped in the only way possible – more indirect taxes, leading to still higher living costs for ordinary Lankans. 

Since the economy is the Government’s Achilles Heel, the Opposition should be shouting from rooftops, accusing the NPP of trying to introduce a policy benefitting a minority of high-earners while ignoring the economic pain of millions of mid and low earners. But the Opposition, which habitually opposes anything the Government does, seems supportive of this particular measure. The Government and the Opposition are also hand-in-glove in resisting IMF pressures to introduce a wealth tax and an inheritance tax for high-earners. 

Why?

The furore around California’s Proposition 40 help explain this curious multi-partisan consensus. Proposition 40 contains a proposal to impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on the state’s billionaires. In a public letter, six Nobel-winning American economists hailed it as a likely “turning point in the battle between democracy and oligarchy.” Pointing out that billionaires pay only 1.6% in income taxes while the average Californian pays 5-6%, they wrote: “What will allow California to thrive in the future is not letting a handful of billionaires live tax-free; it is adequate public spending on health, education, and public infrastructure, key engines of economic growth to which it is only fair to ask the ultra-wealthy to contribute.” (https://www.commondreams.org/news/nobel-laureates-california-wealth-tax),

California’s billionaires are fighting the proposal, tooth and nail, understandably. The state’s Republican leaders too are opposed to it, understandably. So are most of the state’s Democratic leaders (including its supposedly-progressive Governor), not-so-understandably. Congressman Ro Khanna, one of only three of the state’s 54-strong congressional delegation supporting the Proposition explained why most of his own party leaders are opposed to a measure which aligns with the Party’s basic principles. “There’s a view that the biggest threat to American democracy is Donald Trump and not winning the House or Senate, and that we would be foolish to kneecap the prominent billionaires who are on our side” (https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2026/10/12/the-battle-to-pass-a-billionaire-tax). In other words, the role of campaign contributions and the vested interests of millionaires and billionaires making them in deciding policy. Be it in the US or Sri Lanka.

Veils of unknowing

A teenaged-boy is working in a chena. His little sister is sitting close by studying. He has given up schooling due to unaffordability. His teacher comes looking for him, exhorting him to return to school, telling him that for ordinary people education is wings. The boy says that he will sacrifice his opportunity at flying to give his sister a chance.

That was the NPP presidential election ad showcasing its promise to build a better education system accessible to all (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yvLZc6F966A). That promise had a particular resonance coming on the heels of the Wickremesinghe administration’s unconscionable decision to impose an 18% VAT on hitherto tax-free category of books and educational materials. The NPP/JVP roundly criticised the decision. Two years on, books and educational materials continue to be taxed at 18%.

Since the economy is the Government’s Achilles Heel, the Opposition should be shouting from rooftops, accusing the NPP of trying to introduce a policy benefitting a minority of high-earners while ignoring the economic pain of millions of mid and low earners. But the Opposition, which habitually opposes anything the Government does, seems supportive of this particular measure. The Government and the Opposition are also hand-in-glove in resisting IMF pressures to introduce a wealth tax and an inheritance tax for high-earners. Why?

Shortly before taxing books, the Wickremesinghe administration granted China’s Colombo Port Logistics Centre a generous 15-year tax exemption on income and dividends. In January 2026, the NPP Government approved a scheme granting 15-year tax holidays to billion dollar investments in the Port City.

At a June 2026 seminar on taxation, KPMG Sri Lanka head of Tax and Regulatory Suresh Perera warned that Lankan policymakers “are in the dark” on new global investment rules which nullify the tax breaks granted by the BOI and Port City (https://www.ft.lk/top-story/Govt--in-the-dark-as-FDI-tax-incentives-become-obsolete/26-794423). He was referring to the Global Anti-Base Erosion rule (GloBe) known as Pillar Two adopted by the OECD in 2021. It introduced a global minimum tax rate of 15% on corporate profits of all multinationals with global revenues of at least 750 million euros in two of the last four fiscal years. If such a multinational company is given a tax holiday in Sri Lanka, that unpaid tax of 15% would be collected from its parent company by the country in which it is located (https://www.moodys.com/web/en/us/insights/public-sector/understanding-pillar-two-the-global-minimum-tax-policy.html).

The program was supposed to be time-bound, but cannot be because the Government has so far failed to create an effective path out of poverty for its recipients. This lack is exacerbated by the Government’s inability to understand the value of the informal sector in the lives of the poor and the lower middle class. The NPP Government seems to regard the informal sector not as a necessity which needs to be regularised and gradually incorporated into the formal economy but as an eyesore which needs to be wiped off. While the problems caused by some micro and small informal economic structures need to be addressed, it is also important to understand that this is often the only way out of poverty for many of the Lankan poor.

Even when not threatened by the NPP’s mania with surface beautification (an obsession they share with Gotabaya Rajapaksa), these workers exist at a very precarious level, vulnerable to any passing economic wind. These people cannot be forcefully herded into the manufacturing sector, as some politicians suggest. title: Sri Lanka’s Counterterrorism Bill retains abusive powers | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 7 October 2026 03:22
-     - 11

Human Rights Watch Asia Director Elaine Pearson

Sri Lanka has a grim history of misusing bad counterterrorism laws to commit serious human rights violations, and this bill would do little to stop that from happening again. The Sri Lankan Government should fulfill its international legal obligations and commitments to the EU and other international partners by legislating to end these abuses instead of simply repackaging the same abusive powers in new legislation

- Human Rights Watch Asia Director Elaine Pearson

The Sri Lankan Government’s latest attempt to replace its abusive Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) retains numerous provisions that have enabled serious human rights violations, Human Rights Watch said.

The proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill (PSTB), which will be sent to Parliament on 6 October 2026, includes an overbroad definition of terrorism, inadequate judicial oversight, sweeping powers of search and arrest for the armed forces, and executive authority to curtail freedom of speech, assembly, association, and movement. These provisions neither meet the benchmarks set out by United Nations human rights experts, nor comply with human rights obligations and commitments that Sri Lanka made to the European Union under the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP+), which links trade benefits to human rights conditions.

Human Rights Watch Asia Director Elaine Pearson said:  “Sri Lankan authorities have long used draconian counterterrorism legislation to persecute minorities and target the victims of rights abuses and activists seeking justice and accountability. The proposed law will allow similar abuses, breaching Sri Lanka’s obligations under international law and jeopardising its EU trade benefits.”

Election pledge

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s National People’s Power alliance pledged in its 2024 election manifesto to campaign for the abolition “of all oppressive acts including the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) and ensuring civil rights of people in all parts of the country.” The bill is the proposed replacement for the PTA, which has enabled arbitrary detention, ill-treatment, and torture.

That law—first enacted in 1979 as a “temporary” measure—has been used to target Tamil and Muslim communities, the media, human rights defenders, and others critical of successive Governments, entrenching impunity in Sri Lanka for 46 years. In 2017, Sri Lanka committed to repealing the PTA as a condition for the EU to reinstate its GSP+ status. Since 2018, several attempts to repeal and replace the PTA have failed.

The Government introduced an earlier version of the bill in late 2025, but it was withdrawn and has been reintroduced with some changes following criticism by human rights groups, media, and others. Meanwhile, despite the Government’s pledge to abolish the PTA, the Dissanayake Government continued to use the law. In June 2026 it was used to arrest and detain Sangeethan Ganeshkumar, a 24-year-old Tamil hip-hop artist, in connection with a music video.

According to information provided to the UN by the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka, there were 46 PTA-related detention cases in 2025 and 12 in the first 3 months of 2026. It has at times been used in cases—such as alleged organised crime—that should be addressed using ordinary criminal laws, not counterterrorism authority.

Five prerequisites 

In 2021, UN human rights experts set out five prerequisites to ensure that any proposed counterterrorism law complies with international human rights standards. They include providing a definition of terrorism that complies with international norms to ensure precision and legal certainty, especially when the legislation may affect the rights of freedom of expression, opinion, peaceful assembly, association, and religion or belief; instituting robust measures to prevent and halt arbitrary deprivation of liberty; ensuring measures to prevent torture and enforced disappearance; and enabling overarching due process and fair trial guarantees, including judicial oversight and access to legal counsel. The bill does not meet these standards, Human Rights Watch said.

The draft law includes broad and vague definitions of terrorism and could undermine the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. The definition of terrorism problematically includes “unduly compelling a Government or an international organisation, to do or to abstain from doing any act.”

Sweeping provision 

The bill also includes a sweeping provision that anyone who, with “intention or knowledge…directly or indirectly,” induces any person to commit, attempt, abet, conspire to commit, or prepare to commit, the offense of “terrorism” by “distributing, circulating,” or providing “a service to others that enables them to obtain, read, listen to or look at a terrorist publication” commits an offense. The risk that this authority could be used to curtail free speech is shown by the repeated use of the PTA to interrogate, arrest, and detain journalists and social media users.

While the definitions of offenses under the bill are overbroad, the bill includes some improvements. It provides that those who engage in protest, advocacy or dissent; industrial or labour action; or humanitarian and medical assistance will not be considered to commit an offense. However, this does not adequately address the dangers contained in other clauses that could result in abuse.

A further serious concern, as with the previous counterterrorism drafts, is that the latest bill provides broad authority to Sri Lanka’s police, armed forces, and coast guard with “reasonable suspicion” to stop, search, question, enter premises, and take suspects into custody without a warrant.

The proposed law enables the inspector general of police or a deputy inspector general of police to obtain an order from the defence secretary to detain a suspect for two months, which can be extended up to a year. A magistrate cannot overturn a detention order, removing effective judicial oversight. Using different provisions under the bill, a person could be held without charge for up to a total of two years.

Some safeguards

The bill provides some safeguards, such as allowing a magistrate to visit approved detention sites without notice, interview detainees, and direct officials to bring detainees before a Judicial Medical Officer if there is suspicion of torture or ill-treatment. The magistrate can also order a change of detention site.

The bill provides for an Independent Review Committee appointed by the Defence Minister to review the “necessity, legality and proportionality” of a detention order within 30 days and recommend to the minister whether it should be confirmed, varied, or revoked. While independent reviews of detention orders could reduce abuses, the committee’s appointment by the minister would place the independence of such scrutiny in doubt.

Finally, the proposed law grants sweeping Government authority to curtail freedom of movement and association, including for the president to proscribe organisations without judicial oversight. The defence secretary is empowered to designate anywhere a “prohibited place,” while a deputy inspector general of police can obtain a court order to restrict an individual’s movement and communications for up to three months. Such broad powers with limited or no judicial oversight would have a chilling effect on free speech, association, assembly, and movement.

The Sri Lankan Government should impose an immediate moratorium on the use of the PTA while it comprehensively amends the PTSB or prepares a new bill that meets international standards, Human Rights Watch said.

 “Sri Lanka has a grim history of misusing bad counterterrorism laws to commit serious human rights violations, and this bill would do little to stop that from happening again,” Pearson said. “The Sri Lankan Government should fulfill its international legal obligations and commitments to the EU and other international partners by legislating to end these abuses instead of simply repackaging the same abusive powers in new legislation.”

Led by Shangri-La Hambantota General Manager Refhan Razeen, Aitken Spence Hotels Vice President Learning and Development Patrick Pereira, Cinnamon Grand Colombo General Manager Nazoomi Azhar, and Shangri-La Dubai former Director – Marketing and Communications and Cinnamon Hotels and Resorts former Director – Brand Marketing and Partnerships Pramukshi Kariyawasam, the committee brought a strong practitioner perspective to the program. Having worked together across previous workplaces and projects, the team was able to combine their respective areas of expertise and create a conference that was deeply rooted in the realities and opportunities facing the hospitality industry.

The discussions moved beyond individual businesses to consider the wider ecosystem required for Sri Lankan hospitality to compete more effectively in an increasingly dynamic global tourism landscape. International perspectives from destinations including Seychelles and the Maldives provided insight into destination leadership, national positioning and industry collaboration, while sessions on AI, revenue management and consumer trends explored the technologies and behaviours reshaping hospitality. These conversations culminated in the Great Reform Debate, which challenged speakers and delegates to consider what needs to change if Sri Lanka is to realise its Vision 2030 ambitions.

A key outcome of IHLC 2026 was the Vision 2030 Declaration and an industry whitepaper, which has already been drafted by academics from APIIT Sri Lanka. Bringing together research and industry perspectives on the future direction of Sri Lankan hospitality, the whitepaper will now be circulated among industry and relevant government stakeholders as a reference to support wider dialogue, policy thinking and future action.

IHLC 2026 Conference Chairman and Shangri-La Hambantota General Manager Refhan Razeen said: “We did not create this conference to celebrate what we have endured. We created it to confront what comes next. Our industry has already proven its resilience. The next chapter is about reimagining how we lead, compete and grow together.”

Beyond the program, IHLC 2026 created opportunities for networking and experience-sharing throughout the day, with Official Hospitality Partner Cinnamon Grand Colombo playing a central role in the delegate experience. The hotel curated a special breakfast to welcome delegates, followed by a showcase of its signature restaurants at lunch and dinner, with individual stations bringing together a wide selection of cuisines and culinary experiences under one roof. Delegates praised the breadth of the selection and quality of the food, making the dining experience an important part of the conference itself. 

IHLC 2026 Vice Chairman and Cinnamon Grand Colombo General Manager Nazoomi Azhar said: “Supporting IHLC 2026 was our way of investing in the people, ideas and conversations that will shape Sri Lanka’s hospitality future. As a leading local hospitality brand, we felt it was our responsibility to support an initiative that brought together the industry’s leaders and created a platform for meaningful dialogue around its future. The response to the conference and the quality of engagement throughout the day reaffirmed the value of bringing the industry together, and we were proud to contribute to an event that was so well received by the hospitality community.”

Institute of Hospitality – Sri Lanka Region Chairman Ramesh Dassanayake said: “Seeing this vision become reality has been incredibly rewarding. My sincere thanks go to our organising committee, partners, speakers and every delegate who made the inaugural International Hospitality Leaders’ Conference such a meaningful success. What we have started through IHLC 2026 is an important conversation for our industry, and I hope the Vision 2030 Declaration and the work that follows will continue to bring our sector together around the opportunities and challenges ahead.” 

IHLC 2026 was proudly powered by Powered by Partner Nestlé Professional also hosted an all-day coffee lounge and introduced its new Nescafé Superiore range. The event was hosted with the support of Platinum Partners CodeGen International and APIIT Sri Lanka; Gold Partners Lion Brewery Ceylon and Rockland Distilleries; and supported by Lakarcade, Celsius, LAUGFS, SriLankan Airlines, Classic Travels, Aitken Spence Travels, Ninewells Hospital, Hameedia and BYD Sri Lanka. Cinnamon Grand Colombo served as Official Hospitality Partner, while Maharaja Media Network was Official Media Partner.

The inaugural IHLC 2026 marks the beginning of an ongoing platform for the Institute of Hospitality – Sri Lanka Region to convene industry leaders, bring international thinking into the local hospitality conversation and support the sector in translating ideas into meaningful action towards 2030.

title: SLAITO honours Past President Harith Perera for his lasting contribution to association and industry | Daily FT

The Sri Lanka Association of Inbound Tour Operators (SLAITO) paid tribute to its Past President, Harith Perera, at its 46th Annual General Meeting held recently at Cinnamon Life City of Dream, recognising his years of service to the Association and his contribution to the development and promotion of Sri Lanka as a tourism destination.

The tribute was delivered by fellow Past President Nishad Wijetunge, who worked closely with Harith during his tenure and later went on to lead the Association himself.

Harith joined the SLAITO Committee in 2009 and served in several positions before being elected President in 2017. He took office at a time when the industry was evolving rapidly and facing new challenges and opportunities.

“From the outset, he approached the responsibility not simply as an honorary position, but as an opportunity to create greater value for the industry, its stakeholders, and the members he represented,” said Wijetunge.

During his Presidency, Harith focused on strengthening industry collaboration and promoting Sri Lanka as a destination. He believed tour operators, hotels, government institutions and tourism authorities needed to work together to present Sri Lanka to the world as a compelling, sustainable and competitive destination.

A central part of his legacy is the growth of Sancharaka Udawa, SLAITO’s flagship event. Under his leadership, the event was developed into a more sustainable platform, with a particular focus on giving MSMEs from across the regions, especially those offering lesser-known tourism products, a wider and more affordable route to broader markets.

He also strengthened engagement between the private sector and the Government, building closer relationships with Ministries and tourism institutions, while advocating for inbound tour operators. He placed strong emphasis on developing human resources, raising service standards and deepening cooperation among tourism associations.

“Sometimes, the greatest achievements are the platforms we create for others, the relationships we build, the opportunities we open for the next generation, and the institutions we leave stronger than we found them. That is why Harith Perera deserves our recognition today,” he said.

Reflecting on their time working together, Wijetunge added that the lessons he learnt from Harith proved invaluable when he later served as President of the Association.

Newly elected SLAITO President Bobby Jordan Hansen said: “It is fitting that we honour Harith at the very meeting where a new committee takes office. The foundations he helped lay, in collaboration, advocacy and support for smaller operators, are ones we intend to build on. As we look ahead, his example reminds us that leadership is measured by what we leave behind for the industry and for Sri Lanka.”

“Harith never saw the Presidency as a title. He saw it as a responsibility to the whole industry” concluded Wijetunge. 

Harith was presented with a token of appreciation in recognition of his service by SLAITO President Bobby Jordan Hansen and immidiate Past President Nalin Jayasundera.
